title: Place of Supply Errors in GST: How to Identify and Correct Tax Head Mistakes
seoTitle: Fixing Place of Supply Errors in GST Billing
metaDescription: Learn how to identify and fix Place of Supply Errors in GST. Understand IGST vs CGST/SGST rules, Section 77 refunds, and how to amend GSTR-1 invoices.
primaryKeyword: Place of Supply Errors in GST
secondaryKeywords: GST place of supply rules for goods and services
Bill-to Ship-to GST place of supply
GST refund for wrong tax head
intro: One of the most frequent challenges for Indian small businesses is accurately determining the tax head for an invoice. A common mistake occurs when a seller applies CGST and SGST to a transaction that should have carried IGST, or vice versa. These Place of Supply Errors in GST often stem from a misunderstanding of where a supply is legally deemed to have occurred.

The Place of Supply (PoS) is a legal concept that determines whether a transaction is intra-state or inter-state. It is not always the same as the customer's billing address or the shipping destination. When this is misidentified, it leads to the wrong tax being paid to the government, which can disrupt cash flow and cause problems during audits.

For accountants and business owners, catching these errors early is vital. If you have already filed your returns, the law provides specific paths for correction, including amendments and refund claims. This guide explains how to identify these errors, the legal protections available to you, and the steps to rectify your records.

In this article, you will learn the difference between various supply rules, how to handle bill-to ship-to scenarios, and the procedure for claiming refunds under Section 77. We also provide a practical checklist to help you maintain accurate billing records every month.

sections.heading: Understanding Place of Supply: The Foundation of GST Compliance

blocks.text: Place of Supply is the geographical location that determines the tax jurisdiction of a transaction. Under the GST framework, every supply is classified as either intra-state (within the same state) or inter-state (between different states). This classification depends entirely on two factors: the location of the supplier and the legally determined Place of Supply.

Many business owners mistakenly assume that the PoS is always the physical location of the buyer. While this is often true for simple retail sales, complex transactions involving goods in transit, services related to property, or third-party instructions follow different rules. Misidentifying this location is the root cause of most tax head errors.

Special cases exist for Union Territories, where UTGST replaces SGST. Additionally, any supply to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) developer or unit is treated as an inter-state supply, requiring IGST regardless of the physical location of the parties.

sections.heading: Top 5 Place of Supply Mistakes Indian Traders Make

blocks.text: Traders often fall into traps when shipping goods across borders or dealing with multi-state corporate clients. Here are the most frequent errors identified in business audits:
1. The Billing Address Bias
Assuming the customer's head office address is the PoS even when the goods are delivered to a branch in the same state as the supplier. This leads to charging IGST when CGST/SGST was required.
2. Misinterpreting Bill-to Ship-to GST Place of Supply

In a Bill-to Ship-to scenario, the PoS is generally the location of the primary buyer (the one who directed the supply), not the final recipient. If a supplier in Gujarat bills a client in Delhi but ships to a factory in Gujarat, the PoS is Delhi (IGST).
3. E-way Bill and Invoice Mismatch
Entering a different PoS on the E-way bill portal than what is mentioned on the tax invoice creates immediate red flags during transit inspections.
4. Ignoring Installation Rules
For goods that require assembly or installation, the PoS is the site where the installation occurs, regardless of where the buyer is registered.
5. Overlooking SEZ Status
Failing to mark a supply as an SEZ transaction results in charging local taxes instead of the mandatory IGST.

sections.heading: Service Sector Pitfalls: When the Customer’s Address Isn't Enough

blocks.text: Service providers face unique challenges because their 'delivery' is intangible. While the general rule for B2B services is the location of the registered recipient, specific services have 'override' rules.

items: Immovable Property: Services like architecture or interior design are tied to the location of the property. If a Delhi architect works on a site in Mumbai for a Delhi client, the PoS is Maharashtra.
Event Management: The PoS is where the event is physically held. If a Bangalore firm organizes a conference in Goa, the PoS is Goa.
Restaurant and Catering: These are always location-based. A caterer from Punjab serving at a wedding in Haryana must treat the PoS as Haryana.
Training and Performance Appraisal: For unregistered B2C clients, the PoS is where the service is performed.

sections.heading: The Financial Impact: Penalties, Blocked Credits, and Cash Flow Issues

blocks.text: A PoS error is not just a clerical mistake; it has significant financial consequences for both the seller and the buyer.

items: Blocked Input Tax Credit (ITC): If you charge CGST/SGST to a buyer in another state, they cannot claim that tax as credit, increasing their cost by 18% or more.
Double Tax Payment: You may be forced to pay the correct tax head out of pocket while waiting for a refund of the wrong tax paid.
Working Capital Crunch: Refund processes can take months, locking up business funds that could have been used for operations.
Audit Risks: Frequent amendments or PoS errors can trigger scrutiny from tax authorities during annual reconciliations.

sections.heading: Real-Time Correction: Using GSTR-1A Before the GSTR-3B Deadline

blocks.text: The GST portal has introduced the GSTR-1A facility to help taxpayers fix errors quickly. If you discover a PoS mistake after filing GSTR-1 but before filing GSTR-3B, you can use this form to update the tax details.

By correcting the invoice in GSTR-1A, the updated liability (e.g., changing IGST to CGST/SGST) will automatically flow into your GSTR-3B. This prevents the error from being finalized in your monthly payment return, saving you from complex refund applications later.

sections.heading: Amending Past Errors: Navigating Table 9A and Statutory Timelines

blocks.text: If the error is discovered months later, you must use the GSTR-1 invoice amendment process. Table 9A of GSTR-1 is specifically designed for amending B2B invoices that were reported incorrectly in previous periods.

There is a strict deadline for these corrections. Invoices from a previous financial year generally cannot be amended after November 30th of the following financial year. For example, errors made in FY 2023-24 must be corrected by November 30, 2024. Failing to meet this deadline makes the error permanent in the government records.

sections.heading: Paid Tax Under the Wrong Head? Your Rights Under Section 77 & Section 19

blocks.text: The government recognizes that PoS rules are complex. Section 77 of the CGST Act and Section 19 of the IGST Act provide relief for taxpayers who genuinely misclassify a transaction. These sections state that if you paid the wrong tax head, you must pay the correct one, but you are entitled to a refund of the incorrect payment.

A major benefit of these provisions is interest relief. As long as you are reclassifying the tax head (e.g., from IGST to CGST/SGST) and not just paying late, you are not required to pay interest on the 'new' tax liability, provided the original tax was paid on time. This is a crucial protection for businesses caught in technical errors.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Filing for a Refund via RFD-01 for PoS Errors

blocks.text: Once you have paid the correct tax head, you must file a refund claim for the amount paid under the wrong head. This is done using Form GST RFD-01 on the GST Portal.
The workflow for this correction is as follows:

items: Identify the incorrect invoice and the tax period it belongs to.
Pay the correct tax head through a current GSTR-3B or via DRC-03.
Log in to the GST Portal and navigate to the Refunds section.
Select the reason for refund as 'Tax paid on an intra-State supply which is subsequently held to be inter-State supply and vice versa'.
Upload the statement containing details of the original and corrected invoices.
Submit the application and track the Acknowledgement Receipt Number (ARN).

blocks.text: Remember that the time limit for this refund is generally two years from the date of payment of the correct tax. You should maintain a cover letter explaining the nature of the reclassification to speed up the officer's review.

sections.heading: Worked Examples of Place of Supply Corrections

blocks.text: To better understand how these rules apply in real-world scenarios, consider the following illustrative examples.
Example 1: The Misidentified Warehouse

A wholesaler in Rajasthan sells electronics to a retailer who has GST registrations in both Rajasthan and Punjab. The wholesaler mistakenly bills the Punjab GSTIN (IGST) but delivers the goods to the retailer's Rajasthan warehouse. Since the delivery ends in Rajasthan, the PoS is Rajasthan. The wholesaler must amend the invoice to reflect CGST/SGST and the Rajasthan GSTIN of the buyer.
Example 2: Bill-to Ship-to Correction

A manufacturer in Tamil Nadu receives an order from a trader in Maharashtra. The trader asks the manufacturer to ship the goods directly to a customer in Tamil Nadu. The manufacturer initially charges CGST/SGST because the goods stayed in Tamil Nadu. However, under Section 10(1)(b), the PoS is the location of the person directing the supply (Maharashtra). The manufacturer must correct the invoice to IGST.

sections.heading: Audit Checklist: Monthly GST Review for Place of Supply Accuracy

blocks.text: Accountants should perform this brief check before every GSTR-1 filing to minimize errors:

items: Cross-verify the buyer's GSTIN prefix (state code) with the PoS mentioned on the invoice.
Identify all 'Ship-to' addresses that are in a different state than the 'Bill-to' address.
Review all service invoices related to immovable property to ensure PoS matches the property location.
Confirm that all supplies to SEZ units are marked as IGST transactions.
Check that the E-way bill destination state matches the PoS on the tax invoice.
Ensure that for B2C inter-state supplies exceeding a certain value, the name of the state and address of delivery are clearly mentioned.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Billing Address and Place of Supply?
faqs.answer: Billing Address is the physical location of the customer, while Place of Supply is a legal determination under GST law. For instance, in property services, the Place of Supply is where the property is located, even if the customer's billing address is in another state.

faqs.question: Can I claim a refund if I accidentally paid CGST instead of IGST?
faqs.answer: Yes, under Section 77 of the CGST Act, you can claim a refund for tax paid under the wrong head. You must first pay the correct tax (IGST) and then file Form GST RFD-01 to recover the wrongly paid CGST and SGST.

faqs.question: Do I have to pay interest when correcting a tax head error under Section 77?
faqs.answer: No, the law specifically provides that no interest is payable when a supply is subsequently found to have a different classification (intra-state vs inter-state). This relief applies provided the original tax was paid within the due dates.

faqs.question: How do I fix a Place of Supply error in an e-invoice after 24 hours?
faqs.answer: An e-invoice cannot be cancelled after 24 hours on the IRP. You must issue a Credit Note to nullify the incorrect invoice and generate a new e-invoice with the correct Place of Supply, or use the GSTR-1 amendment table if the portal allows.

faqs.question: What is the last date to amend GST invoices for the previous financial year?
faqs.answer: The deadline for amending invoices from the previous financial year is November 30th of the following year. This applies to corrections in GSTR-1 for any errors made between April and March of the preceding year.

faqs.question: Is the Place of Supply different for B2B and B2C service transactions?
faqs.answer: Yes, for B2B services, the PoS is usually the location of the registered recipient. For B2C services, it is often the location of the provider unless the address of the recipient is available on record, or specific rules for property/events apply.

faqs.question: How does Bill-to Ship-to affect the Place of Supply?
faqs.answer: In a Bill-to Ship-to transaction, the Place of Supply is deemed to be the principal place of business of the person who directs the supply. This means the tax head is determined by the location of the 'Bill-to' party, not the 'Ship-to' party.

faqs.question: Can I adjust the wrong tax paid in the next month's GSTR-3B?
faqs.answer: No, you cannot simply adjust one tax head against another (e.g., using CGST credit to pay IGST liability) in GSTR-3B for PoS errors. You must pay the correct head and apply for a refund of the incorrect one through the formal RFD-01 process.
